threads.thread_goal: Align on campaign objectives, target segments, and value proposition

messages.text: Sharing a first draft of the Campaign Strategy and Brief for the printed catalog service. It is in A1 and maps back to T1. Draft primary objective: drive qualified catalog quote requests via the new landing page, with a secondary objective of building a remarketing audience for follow-up offers. For KPIs, I proposed: 1) number of catalog quote requests, 2) cost per quote request, 3) quote-to-opportunity rate from CRM. Target-wise, I outlined two main segments: existing SMB customers who already print with us, and net-new local businesses that still rely on printed materials for sales. Value prop draft: customized, professionally printed catalogs that make it easier for their sales teams to present products offline, with reliable turnaround and support. Looking for feedback before we lock D1 and D2.

Thanks for sharing. From recent conversations, existing SMB customers who already trust us for print tend to move faster on new catalog formats, especially when we can reuse assets. For net-new, I see more education needed around why a printed catalog still matters. For D2, I would lean toward prioritizing existing SMB customers first, and using net-new as a secondary test segment. On KPIs, can we also track time from lead to first sales conversation, so we see if the process is smooth for the sales team?

Agree that existing SMB customers are the lowest friction. I would add a sub-segment: customers who already order brochures or flyers from us. They usually have product images and copy ready, which should shorten catalog setup. For KPIs, could we include a target number of catalog samples requested by prospects during calls? That would help us see if the sales playbook we will build in T5 is actually driving interest.

From my side on calls, the strongest hook has been when we connect catalogs to very concrete use cases: trade shows, field sales visits, and dealer networks. Maybe the value prop in A1 can call out that catalogs help them keep product info consistent across teams, even when internet access is spotty. For KPIs, I like quote-to-opportunity rate, but I would also like a simple target for how many catalog discussions each rep should have per week once leads start coming in.

On the print side, I want to make sure the value prop does not overpromise. For example, we can do high-quality color catalogs, but some advanced finishes are limited. In A1, could we phrase it more around reliable color and consistent quality, and less around very special effects? That will keep us aligned with what we can actually produce later when we detail specs in A3 and T3.

Good points. I can update A1 so the primary segment is existing SMB print customers, with a focus on those already ordering brochures or flyers, and keep net-new local businesses as a secondary test segment. For KPIs, I will add: 1) time from lead to first sales conversation, 2) number of catalog discussions per rep per week, and 3) number of catalog sample requests. These will sit under the main objective of driving qualified catalog quote requests. Once I update the brief, I will share a short summary here so we can close D1 and D2.

One more nuance for the value prop: can we highlight that we help them structure their product information, not just print it? In practice, we often guide customers on how to group products and choose key specs. That is a real differentiator versus generic printers. As long as we do not frame it as a full design agency service, it should be safe from a promise standpoint.

Yes, we can support with layout suggestions and basic structure, but we should avoid saying we do full custom design from scratch. Maybe in A1 we can say that we provide guidance on catalog layout and print-ready preparation, and keep the more complex design work as an optional, scoped service if needed.

On the objective, do we want to set a numeric target for the first 30 days? For example, X catalog quote requests and a maximum cost per quote request. That would help when we later build the media plan in A2 and T2, so we can back into required traffic and conversion rates.

Agree we should be concrete. Based on budget ranges we have been discussing for A2, I suggest we set an initial target of 80 to 100 catalog quote requests in the first 30 days, with a cost per quote request not exceeding our current average for print leads. I will translate that into traffic and conversion assumptions in T2. If no one objects, I will write these into A1 as the primary objective and numeric KPIs.

Those numbers sound reasonable from a sales capacity standpoint. If we hit 80 to 100 quote requests, we can handle the follow-up as long as the lead routing in T6 is clear. For the value prop, I will make sure the sales playbook in A4 mirrors the same promises you lock into A1, so we do not create confusion between marketing and sales messaging.

I have updated A1 now: 1) Primary objective: generate 80 to 100 qualified catalog quote requests in the first 30 days of the campaign, at or below our current average cost per print lead. 2) KPIs: catalog quote requests, cost per quote request, quote-to-opportunity rate, time from lead to first sales conversation, catalog discussions per rep per week, and catalog sample requests. 3) Priority segments: a) existing SMB print customers, especially those already ordering brochures or flyers, b) secondary test: net-new local businesses that rely on printed materials. 4) Value prop: we provide customized, professionally printed catalogs with reliable color and consistent quality, plus guidance on catalog layout and print-ready preparation, without promising full custom design. Unless there are strong objections, I propose we treat this as our baseline and mark D1 and D2 as agreed so we can move on to T2.
The updated summary in A1 looks good to me. The segment focus and KPIs match what we can realistically support on the sales side. I am fine with closing D1 and D2 based on this version.
No objections from me. The numeric targets and segment priorities are clear, and they will help when we build the media plan in A2. Happy to proceed with D1 and D2 as summarized.
From the production side, the way you framed the value prop in A1 is safe in terms of what we can deliver. I am aligned with closing D1 and D2 so we can move on to the creative and spec work in T3.

threads.thread_goal: Lock channel mix, budget split, and launch timeline

messages.text: I have drafted the initial media plan in A2, based on the objectives and segments we aligned in A1 and T1. Proposed channel mix for T2 and T10: 40 percent paid social (Facebook and Instagram), 35 percent paid search, 15 percent email to existing customers, and 10 percent reserved for retargeting. Budget stays within the cap we discussed with marketing. For timing, I am proposing a go-live date 14 days from today, which keeps us inside the 21-day window and leaves a week for pre-launch QA and tracking checks from T7. Please review the split and the date so we can converge on D3 and D4.

Looking at A2, I like the emphasis on paid search for intent-driven leads. For existing SMB customers, email plus retargeting should be strong. One question: is 10 percent for retargeting enough if we want to build a solid remarketing audience early? Maybe we can shift a bit from paid social prospecting to retargeting without breaking the top-of-funnel too much.

From a sales perspective, the 14-day go-live works, as long as we have enough time to finalize A4 and A6 and run at least one short training session from T9 before launch. On channel mix, I would not reduce paid search too much, but I am open to slightly increasing retargeting if we see early traction in the first 72 hours of T10.

Agree on the 14-day timeline. It gives us a clear date to work toward for the sales playbook and workflow. For channels, I would just ask that we have enough volume from existing customers via email so we can quickly test the sales scripts in A4 and refine them before we scale prospecting too much.

On the production side, the 14-day go-live is ok, but I want to flag that we need enough time for pre-launch QA in T8 and to run through the checklist in A5. If creatives come in late, we might have to rush checks on print claims. So I would prefer that we lock the date but keep a clear cut-off for creative changes a few days before launch.

Good call on retargeting. How about we adjust the mix to: 35 percent paid social prospecting, 35 percent paid search, 20 percent email, and 10 percent retargeting for the first week. Then, based on early performance from T10 and the tracking in A7, we can reallocate up to 10 percent more into retargeting if we see strong engagement. That way we do not overcommit before we have data.

That phased approach works for me. As long as we have the flexibility to shift budget quickly once we see which segment responds best, we should be fine. Just make sure the UTM structure in T7 lets us distinguish existing customers from net-new leads clearly.

Yes, in A7 I will define UTMs that tag both channel and audience type, so we can see performance by existing vs net-new. For the email share, I kept it at 20 percent to avoid overloading the list in the first weeks, but we can schedule a second wave if the first performs well.

On the go-live date, can we be explicit about the day of the week? Launching mid-week usually gives us better early read for B2B. If 14 days from now lands on a weekend, I would suggest we shift to the following Monday but still stay within the 21-day window.

I checked the calendar: 14 days from today is a Thursday. That should work well for B2B. We can plan to activate campaigns in the morning and monitor closely for the first 72 hours as part of T10. If we all agree, we can lock that Thursday as the official launch date for D4.

Thursday launch works for me. That gives us the earlier part of the week to finish QA in T8 and run through A5. I just need final creatives at least three business days before that Thursday to do proper checks on print specs and claims.

From sales, Thursday is fine. We can schedule the training in T9 earlier that same week so everyone is ready when leads start coming in. No concerns on the channel mix as long as we get visibility into which leads are coming from which channel in the CRM.

I am aligned with the updated split: 35 percent paid social, 35 percent search, 20 percent email, 10 percent retargeting to start. That gives us enough coverage across the funnel. I am ok marking D3 as agreed based on that distribution and the Thursday launch for D4.

Summarizing so we are all on the same page: 1) Channel mix for launch (D3): 35 percent paid social prospecting, 35 percent paid search, 20 percent email to existing customers, 10 percent retargeting, with flexibility to shift up to 10 percent more into retargeting after the first 72 hours based on T10 results. 2) Launch date (D4): campaigns go live on the Thursday that is 14 days from today, with a three-business-day cut-off for creative changes to allow T8 and A5 QA. I will update A2 and A7 accordingly and start setting up T7 and T10.

threads.thread_goal: Validate creative concepts against print capabilities and finalize specs

messages.text: I have gone through the early creative mockups and the current draft of the Creative and Print Specification Guide in A3, linked back to T3. Overall, the visuals look strong, but I see a few areas where we need to adjust claims and specs so they match what we can actually produce. For example, some ads mention very fast turnaround and special finishes that are not standard. I have added comments in A3, but wanted to walk through them here so we can finalize guidelines and move toward D5 and D6.

Thanks for the review. On the turnaround claim, I had used a generic fast wording to keep the ads punchy. Can you clarify in A3 what we can safely promise as a standard turnaround window for the catalog formats we are targeting? Once we lock that, I will update the copy in T4 and send it for compliance review.

For standard catalogs with the page counts we are planning, a safe promise is delivery within a typical business turnaround that includes production and shipping. We should avoid very aggressive timelines in the ads. In A3, I suggested wording like reliable turnaround with clear timelines confirmed at quote stage. That way sales can give specific dates case by case without us overcommitting in the creative.

From the sales side, I support that approach. When we get into specifics with customers, there are often variables like page count and finishing that affect timing. If the ads and landing page keep it at reliable turnaround and we confirm exact dates during the quote, it keeps expectations realistic. For D6, I would lean toward promoting core features like high-quality color, consistent print, and flexible page counts, and leave more complex finishes as optional add-ons we mention only in the sales conversation.

Agree. When we oversell special finishes in marketing, we end up spending a lot of time explaining limitations on calls. If A3 clearly lists which finishes are standard and which are custom, we can mirror that in A4 and keep the ads focused on the standard offer. That should also make the FAQ in T5 easier to write.

One more thing: some mockups show very thick paper stock. Can we confirm in A3 what paper weights we want to feature in the visuals? If we show something that looks premium but the base offer is lighter, customers might feel misled. I would rather we show what most customers will actually receive.

Good catch. In A3 I can specify a default paper range for the visuals that matches our standard catalog offer. We can still mention premium paper as an upgrade in the sales materials, but the main creatives should reflect the standard. I will add that to the spec list in T3.

Understood. I will adjust the ad and landing page copy in T4 to remove any hard turnaround promises and use the reliable turnaround wording you suggested. For D6, based on this discussion, I propose we promote: 1) high-quality color catalogs, 2) consistent print quality across runs, 3) flexible page counts within a defined range, and 4) guidance on layout and print-ready preparation. We will not promote special finishes or ultra-fast delivery in the main ads.
That list of promoted features works well for sales conversations. It sets a clear baseline and leaves room to upsell when appropriate. I am comfortable treating that as our decision for D6.
Same here. If A3 and A4 both reflect those four core features, we will have a consistent story from ad to call. That should also reduce back-and-forth with customers about what is included.

I have now updated A3 with: 1) standard catalog sizes and page count ranges, 2) default paper weights for visuals, 3) safe wording on turnaround, and 4) a clear split between standard and custom finishes. I also added a short checklist that we can reuse in A5 and T8 for pre-launch QA. If everyone is ok with this version, I suggest we mark D5 as approved for the creative and print spec guidelines.

I reviewed the latest A3 and it covers what we need. The spec list is clear enough for the creative team, and the checklist will help us avoid last-minute surprises in T8. I am fine marking D5 as approved and will align all copy and creatives in T4 to these guidelines.
Confirmed from my side as well. The separation between standard and custom options in A3 will make it easier to explain the offer to customers. Happy to close D5 and D6 based on this.

threads.thread_goal: Finalize sales playbook, lead workflow, and training approach

messages.text: I have uploaded a draft of the Sales Playbook and FAQ in A4 and the Lead Handling Workflow and SLA Matrix in A6, both tied to T5 and T6. The playbook covers: 1) positioning of the printed catalog service aligned with A1 and A3, 2) a call structure for discovery and scoping, 3) objection handling, and 4) a 15-question FAQ. The workflow in A6 defines routing rules from the online form to the right rep, plus response time targets. Looking for feedback so we can finalize structure and messaging for D7 and confirm routing and SLAs for D8.

I went through A4. The structure is clear, especially the discovery questions. One suggestion: in the opening, can we add a short line that connects back to the online ad or email they saw? That usually helps build continuity. Also, in the FAQ, we might want to add a question about how often they can update their catalog, since that comes up a lot.

On A6, I like that leads from existing customers go directly to their current account owner. For net-new leads, you have them going into a shared queue with a 4-business-hour response target. Given the campaign focus, I would push for a 2-business-hour target during working hours, at least for the first month, so we can maximize conversion while interest is fresh.

From a marketing side, the messaging in A4 is well aligned with A1 and A3. Just a couple of tweaks: 1) in the benefits section, please remove any mention of ultra-fast turnaround and stick to reliable timelines, and 2) in the section about finishes, make sure we clearly label which options are standard versus custom, matching A3. Once we finalize wording, I will reuse some of the FAQ content in the landing page brief from T4.

In A4, under technical questions, there is a line that suggests we can always handle very high page counts without extra checks. I would soften that. For very large catalogs, we sometimes need to review specs more carefully. Maybe we can say that higher page counts are possible but may require a custom quote and timeline.

Good suggestions. I will add an opening line that references the ad or email they came from, so reps can say something like: you requested more info after seeing our catalog campaign. I will also add a FAQ entry about how often they can update their catalog, with guidance on reprints and minor updates versus full redesigns.

On the SLA in A6, I am comfortable tightening net-new lead response to 2 business hours during working hours for the first month. We will need to make sure everyone is aware of this in the T9 training. I will update the matrix to reflect that and keep 4 hours as a fallback outside peak times.

I will adjust the benefits section in A4 to remove any strong promises on speed and align with the reliable turnaround wording from A3. I will also clearly mark standard versus custom finishes in the feature list, so it matches what we promote in the ads and landing page.

Good point on high page counts. I will update that FAQ answer in A4 to say that larger catalogs are possible but may require a custom quote and timeline, and that reps should check with production for edge cases.

On the workflow in A6, can we also tag leads by channel and segment so we can later analyze response times and conversion by source in T12? If that is feasible within our current CRM setup, it will help us refine both the media plan and the sales process.

Yes, we can add fields in the CRM to capture channel and segment, and map them from the UTM parameters defined in A7. I will coordinate with the CRM owner to make sure the routing rules in A6 use those fields without breaking existing flows.

I have now incorporated all the feedback into A4 and A6: 1) Playbook structure: intro referencing the campaign, discovery questions, positioning aligned with A1 and A3, objection handling, and an expanded FAQ with at least 15 questions, including catalog updates and high page counts. 2) Workflow: existing customers routed to their account owner, net-new leads to a shared queue with a 2-business-hour response target during working hours, plus tagging by channel and segment. Unless there are concerns, I propose we treat this as our final structure and messaging for D7 and our confirmed routing and SLAs for D8.
The updated A4 and A6 look solid. The call structure is practical, and the 2-hour SLA is ambitious but doable if we plan schedules accordingly. I am comfortable marking D7 and D8 as agreed.
Aligned from marketing as well. The messaging in A4 is consistent with A1 and A3, and the workflow in A6 will give us the data we need for T10 and T12. Happy to close D7 and D8 based on your summary.
From production, I am ok with the way technical limits are described in A4. It sets the right expectations on page counts and finishes. No further changes from my side.

threads.thread_goal: Review early performance, customer feedback, and next optimizations

messages.text: We are 5 days into the campaign, so I have pulled an initial snapshot and drafted a first version of the Post-Launch Performance and Insights Report in A8, based on tracking and reporting requirements from A7 and T10. High level: 1) We have 32 catalog quote requests so far, slightly below the linear pace for our 80 to 100 target. 2) Cost per quote request is close to our current print lead average. 3) Paid search is driving most of the qualified leads, while paid social is generating more top-of-funnel traffic but lower conversion. I would like to review these results together and combine them with early customer feedback from T11 before we lock in any major optimizations.

On the sales side, from the first batch of leads, I have spoken with 6 customers and logged notes for T11. The strongest positive feedback is about having a single, structured document for their sales teams. A few prospects mentioned they were not fully clear on how often they can update the catalog, but the FAQ in A4 helped once we explained it. One concern: a couple of leads expected more advanced finishes because of what they had seen from other vendors, even though our ads did not promise that. We might want to emphasize our standard offer more clearly in follow-up emails.

I have had 4 catalog discussions so far. The 2-hour SLA in A6 is working; we are usually getting back to leads within that window. However, some leads from paid social seem less ready to commit and need more education. Maybe we can adjust the retargeting creative to include a short explainer about the process, using some of the content from A4.

From my calls, the main friction point has been uncertainty about pricing for different page counts and paper options. Once we walk them through the standard offer, most are fine, but it takes time. Maybe we can add a simple pricing range example to the landing page or follow-up email, without going into full rate card detail.

On the production side, the first catalog jobs coming through look aligned with A3. No major issues with specs so far. One small pattern: a few customers are sending images that are too low resolution. Maybe we can highlight the image quality requirement more clearly in the landing page and in the FAQ, so we reduce back-and-forth on file replacements.

Thanks for the feedback. In A8, I will add a section summarizing these early customer reactions from T11. For the advanced finishes expectation, we can test a follow-up email variant that explicitly states what is included in the standard catalog package and mentions that custom finishes are available on request. That should set expectations without adding friction.

On paid social, the data in A7 shows a lot of clicks but lower form completion. I agree that more education could help. I will propose a retargeting creative that uses a simple three-step visual: share your product info, we help structure the catalog, you receive printed copies. I will also check if we can reuse some of the explainer language from A4 in the landing page.

Pricing clarity is a good call-out. We need to stay within what legal and compliance allow, but we might be able to add a starting-from range and a couple of example scenarios to the landing page brief in T4. I will check with the marketing manager and compliance before we change any public pricing language.

On image quality, we can also add a short script in A4 for reps to use when they first talk to customers: a reminder about recommended resolution and file formats. That way we reinforce the message both online and in the call.
That would help. I can also add a simple visual example in A3 that shows the difference between low and high resolution, which we can link from the FAQ or landing page if needed.

Looking at the numbers in A8, do we see any clear difference in lead quality between existing customers and net-new? My impression is that existing customers are moving faster to quotes, but I want to confirm with data before we suggest any budget shifts.

Yes, the early data in A8 shows that existing customers have a higher quote-to-opportunity rate and shorter time from lead to first conversation. Net-new leads are cheaper on paid social but convert to quotes at a lower rate. For now, I suggest we keep the current channel mix but shift a small portion of paid social budget toward audiences that look more like our existing customers, and monitor the impact over the next week.

For T11, I will continue to log detailed notes from the next set of customer calls, focusing on: 1) how they heard about the campaign, 2) what convinced them to request a catalog, and 3) any confusion about specs or pricing. I will share a short summary before the end of the week so you can incorporate it into A8.

That adjustment sounds reasonable. As long as we keep a clear view in A7 of which leads are coming from which audience, we can decide later whether to double down on existing-customer lookalikes or keep a broader net.

I have updated A8 with: 1) performance by channel and segment, 2) early customer feedback from T11, including expectations on finishes, pricing clarity, and catalog update frequency, and 3) proposed next steps: a) test a more educational retargeting creative, b) clarify standard vs custom offer in follow-up emails, c) explore adding simple pricing examples and stronger image quality guidance to the landing page and FAQ, pending compliance review. I will continue to refresh A8 twice a week as more data and feedback come in.
